analysis.one_liner: Funds free lawyers for low-income tenants facing eviction.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would give states and cities $100 million a year to cover lawyers for low-income tenants in eviction court, was introduced in July 2025 and has seen no action since it was sent to the Senate Banking Committee.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill creates an Eviction Right to Counsel Fund. The federal government would offer $100 million a year for five years to states, cities, and tribal governments that pass laws guaranteeing a free lawyer to tenants earning up to twice the federal poverty level who are facing eviction or losing a housing subsidy. It gives extra points in the grant competition to places that also limit no-fault evictions, require at least 30 days' notice, set up eviction diversion programs, or provide emergency rental assistance.
analysis.who_benefits: Low-income tenants facing eviction or the loss of a housing subsidy — the bill covers tenants earning up to 200% of the federal poverty line — would get a lawyer at no cost in eviction court. State and local governments that adopt right-to-counsel laws would get federal money to pay for it, and the legal aid programs that hire and train those attorneys would gain funded work. Studies cited in right-to-counsel debates nationally have found represented tenants far more likely to stay in their homes.

how_it_helps.text: Creates an Eviction Right to Counsel Fund and authorizes $100 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 in grants to states, local governments, and tribal governments.

Grants go only to governments that enact legislation guaranteeing full legal representation, at no cost, to tenants earning up to 200% of the federal poverty line in eviction cases and housing-subsidy termination cases.

In awarding grants, HUD must prioritize governments that also limit the grounds for no-fault eviction, require at least 30 days' written notice, run eviction diversion programs, or provide emergency rental assistance.
Grant money can pay the actual costs of providing the representation, including training and recruiting attorneys for tenants.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through up to $500 million in appropriations over five years. Landlords in jurisdictions that take the grants and tighten their eviction laws would bear higher costs and longer timelines to remove tenants, since represented tenants more often contest evictions successfully.

drawbacks.text: The bill authorizes up to $500 million over five years in new federal spending, and grants flow only to governments that first pass their own right-to-counsel laws, so tenants in states that choose not to act get nothing.

The grant incentives push participating governments toward limiting no-fault evictions and requiring 30-day notice, which landlords argue raises their costs and delays reclaiming their property, particularly from tenants who genuinely stopped paying rent.
Because the bill is an incentive rather than a mandate, it would create a patchwork: a tenant's right to a lawyer would depend on where they live.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the roughly several hundred million dollars over five years, the bill would extend legal representation to a population that almost always faces eviction court alone today, and represented tenants are substantially more likely to keep their housing. The main honest objections are that the money reaches only states and cities that opt in, and that the federal cost is real, though small relative to the human stakes of eviction. The design leans on voluntary state action, which limits its reach but also its price tag.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee in July 2025, and it has sat there with no hearing, no markup, and no floor vote since.

narrative.text: Sen. Cory Booker introduced the Eviction Right to Counsel Act of 2025 in the Senate on July 24, 2025, joined by Democratic Senators Van Hollen, Wyden, Blumenthal and Independent Senator Sanders.
The same day, the bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs.
The bill authorizes $100 million per year for fiscal years 2026 through 2030 for grants to state, local, and tribal governments that guarantee free lawyers to low-income tenants in eviction cases.
No further action — no committee vote, hearing, or floor consideration — appears in the bill's action history after the referral.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far, no one has gained or lost anything concrete: the bill is pending, with no vote taken. If it stalls the way similar bills have, landlords and jurisdictions that prefer not to fund tenant representation are better off, because the incentive grants would never arrive.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, nobody — bill sits idle

for.name: Cory Booker
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill and introduced it in the Senate on July 24, 2025.

for.name: Chris Van Hollen, Ron Wyden, Richard Blumenthal, Bernie Sanders
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill at introduction, the only four senators to do so.

against.name: Senate Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on July 24, 2025 and has taken no further action on it — no hearing or markup is listed in the action history.

sides.party_line_note: All five sponsors are Democrats or allied independents, and no Republican has signed on; no votes have occurred, so the partisan split on the merits is untested.

industries.note: The bill pays for tenant lawyers in jurisdictions that adopt right-to-counsel laws, which makes evictions slower and more contested, and it steers extra grant money to places that limit no-fault evictions and require 30-day notice. Landlords would face higher legal costs and longer timelines to recover their units, which is precisely the cost tenants' representation is meant to impose.
Grant money would fund representation for tenants and pay for training and recruiting eviction-defense attorneys, expanding funded work in this field. Their interest runs directly alongside tenants'.

analysis.trajectory: The bill sits in the Senate Banking Committee with no scheduled hearing or markup and no Republican cosponsors, in a Republican-controlled Senate. Bills referred to committee without bipartisan sponsorship and without committee action in their first year overwhelmingly die when the Congress ends. Unless the committee acts, this bill is on a path to expire without a vote in January 2027.
